outsourcing.def: Hiring another firm to do part of a company's work, often in another country where costs are lower (offshoring).

deindustrialization.def: The decline of factory jobs and industry in a region, as factories close, move away or replace workers with machines.

newly-industrialized-country.def: A country whose economy has shifted quickly from farming toward factories and exports, such as South Korea from the 1960s.

special-economic-zone.def: An area with lower taxes, fewer rules and cheaper land for firms making goods for export, such as Shenzhen, China. Free-trade zones, export-processing zones and Mexico's maquiladoras are related forms.

international-division-of-labor.def: The split of the stages of making a product among different countries, by their skills and costs.

post-fordism.def: Flexible production in smaller batches, spread among many firms and places, with just-in-time delivery; it followed Fordism, the mass production of identical goods on assembly lines in one large plant.

multiplier-effect.def: The way new jobs in one industry create more jobs in others, as workers spend wages and suppliers grow; it also works in reverse when a plant closes.

agglomeration.def: The clustering of many firms in one place because being close lets them share workers, suppliers, services and ideas.

just-in-time.def: Delivering parts to a factory just when they are needed, so little stock is kept.

growth-pole.def: A key industry or major investment, often planned, whose growth spreads to the region around it through the multiplier effect.
